shots.text: Telling individual animals apart means comparing the markings in two photos. Image matchers already do this: they find keypoints and connect the ones that correspond.
But these matchers were trained on buildings and streets, not on fur, and wildlife datasets have no keypoint labels to retrain them.
What every monitoring project does have is identity labels: which photos show the same animal. WildMatch uses nothing else.

The pretrained matcher scores each photo against the rest. Its highest-scoring photos of the same animal become positives. Its highest-scoring photos of other animals become hard negatives: the pairs it gets wrong.
Training then asks for one thing: the score with a positive must beat the score with a hard negative by a margin. Only the matching module changes; the keypoints and descriptors stay as they were.
After adaptation the matcher finds many more correspondences on the animal, and photos of the right individual fill the top of the candidate list.
Across eight wildlife datasets, accuracy improves with about five GPU-hours of training, and every match can be inspected, line by line.
